raw_text:
**Introduction**

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, causing substantial morbidity, mortality, and economic strain despite the rapid progression of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [1–3]. Device-based interventions, particularly cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), have significantly improved survival and reduced hospitalization rates in a subset of patients [2]. However, CRT is indicated only for patients who exhibit prolonged QRS duration (typically $\ge130$ ms) and ventricular dyssynchrony [2,3]. Up to 70% of symptomatic HF patients present with a narrow QRS duration ($\le120$ ms) and are thus ineligible for resynchronization [4,5]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as an innovative, bioelectronic device-based therapy designed to address this therapeutic gap. CCM enhances myocardial function without requiring biventricular resynchronization, offering a valuable option for medically refractory patients [1].

**Mechanisms of Action**

CCM therapy involves delivering relatively high-voltage (approximately 7.5 V), long-duration (approximately 20 ms), biphasic electrical signals to the right ventricular septal wall during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [1,4]. Because these electrical impulses are non-excitatory, they do not trigger a new depolarization or alter cardiac rhythm [4,5]. Preclinical evaluations in isolated cardiomyocyte models [6] and chronic canine models of HF [7] have demonstrated that CCM acutely increases the rate of left ventricular (LV) pressure rise ($dP/dt_{\max}$) without elevating myocardial oxygen consumption ($MVO_2$). This is a crucial distinction from traditional positive inotropic drugs, which increase $MVO_2$ and are associated with adverse long-term outcomes [8]. 

At the cellular level, CCM directly modulates calcium cycling. In the short term, CCM restores calcium handling by increasing intracellular calcium transits and upregulating the expression and phosphorylation of sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA2a) and phospholamban [9,10]. Over intermediate and longer periods of treatment, these cellular adaptations shift abnormally expressed genes associated with the fetal gene program back toward adult patterns [9,10]. These beneficial molecular changes extend globally, promoting reverse LV structural remodeling and restoring longitudinal strain [11].

**Clinical Trial Evidence**

The safety and efficacy of CCM have been established through a series of prospective clinical trials. Early feasibility studies and the crossover-designed FIX-HF-4 trial demonstrated significant safety and clinical benefits [5,12,13]. In the subsequent randomized, unblinded FIX-HF-5 trial of 428 patients, CCM led to notable improvements in exercise capacity, as measured by peak oxygen consumption (peak $VO_2$), and health-related quality of life compared with optimal medical therapy alone [14,15]. The subsequent pivotal, randomized, controlled FIX-HF-5C trial used Bayesian statistical methods to confirm significant gains in exercise capacity, functional status, and quality of life, alongside a reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalizations [16]. 

Initially, the Optimizer device required three leads (one atrial lead for synchronization and two ventricular leads for signal delivery). However, technology has evolved to the 2-lead Optimizer Smart system, which eliminates the atrial lead, simplifies the surgical implantation procedure, and maintains the clinical efficacy of previous systems [17]. Furthermore, clinical investigations have proven the feasibility and safety of CCM in patients with permanent atrial fibrillation (AF) by adjusting signal delivery parameters [18].

**Survival, Registries, and Real-World Evidence**

Long-term survival and real-world outcomes of CCM are supported by prospective clinical registries and single-center cohorts. Retrospective studies in Europe have shown a clinical responder rate of over 70% and a significant increase in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) at long-term follow-up [19]. Kloppe et al. observed that mortality rates in patients treated with CCM were significantly lower than predicted by the Seattle Heart Failure Model [20]. Furthermore, the large, prospective CCM-REG registry, evaluating 503 patients from 51 European centers, demonstrated sustained improvements in New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, quality of life, and LVEF over a 24-month period [21]. Meta-analyses of randomized trials have consistently confirmed significant improvements in peak $VO_2$, 6-minute walk distance, and health-related quality of life [22–25].

**Advanced Applications and Guidelines**

CCM has also been investigated in complex clinical contexts. Kuschyk et al. demonstrated that CCM is a viable option for patients who do not respond to biventricular pacing, indicating that contractility enhancement can complement resynchronization [25]. Furthermore, combining CCM with subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (S-ICD) was shown to be safe and free from adverse device-device interactions [26]. While initial research focused on HFrEF, pilot data from the CCM-HFpEF study suggest that CCM can also improve health status and quality of life in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [27]. 

In response to this growing evidence base, both European [2,28] and American guidelines [3,28] recognize CCM as a therapeutic option (Class IIb) to improve functional capacity and quality of life. The device implantation is straightforward, requiring standard transvenous pacing techniques [29], and recent technical updates have minimized complications [30]. CCM represents a crucial therapeutic tool for patients with symptomatic, medically refractory heart failure and a narrow QRS.
